Chapter 7: Listening Deeply—The Art of Understanding Before Responding.
Let’s be honest—once a conversation really gets going, it’s easy to think your next move should be persuading the other person. But, the most powerful thing you can do isn’t to convince... it’s to truly listen.
Deep listening goes way beyond just hearing someone’s words. It’s about tuning in, really soaking up their story, their emotions, and what they need—sometimes even the things they aren’t saying out loud. When you listen at this level, you create a safe space. The other person feels validated, and suddenly, it’s possible to go past those surface-level disagreements.
So, how do you actually listen deeply? Here are a few things you can try:
First, give your full attention. Seriously—put your phone away, let go of your own thoughts for a moment, and just focus on the other person, both with your words and your body language.
Next, reflect back what you’re hearing. That could sound like, “So you’re saying you felt left out of the decision?” It’s a simple way to show you get it.
Then, acknowledge emotions. Sometimes, people don’t say exactly how they’re feeling, but you can still notice and name it. Maybe you say, “It sounds like this has been really frustrating for you.” That kind of recognition can mean the world.
And finally, ask open-ended questions. Instead of trying to lead the conversation, invite them to share more. You might ask, “Can you tell me more about what that was like for you?”
Let’s make it real for a second. Imagine a parent and a teenager arguing over curfew. The parent’s worried about safety, while the teen just wants some freedom. If the parent listens deeply, they might pick up on the teen’s need for independence—and even some hidden feelings of mistrust. Now, this doesn’t mean the parent has to agree with everything. It just means they’re showing that the teen’s experience matters.
Deep listening is a bit like holding up a mirror. When people feel seen and heard, their defenses start to drop. They’re more likely to open up and be honest. Plus, it helps clear up misunderstandings and brings out the real issues hiding underneath.
It’s totally normal to want to jump in with your own solutions or arguments. But if you hit pause and listen first, you’ll notice the conversation usually goes better. When both sides feel understood, you can move from butting heads to actually working together.
